summary:
Dominica's High Court of Justice in Roseau struck sections 14 and 16 of the Sexual Offences Act on 23 April 2024, holding the provisions that criminalised consensual same-sex activity unconstitutional. The case was brought by a gay man living in Dominica, and as a result consensual same-sex conduct between adults is no longer an offence under the statute.

The repeal came through judicial review rather than through an act of parliament: the High Court determined that the sections were unconstitutional, so the change rests on a court judgment instead of legislative repeal.

Human Rights Watch reported the decision on 24 April 2024 and called on all Caribbean nations to repeal comparable criminal laws, placing the ruling against a regional pattern in which such statutes remain in force.

The provisions had been under constitutional challenge before the 2024 judgment. MiRiDom founder Daryl Phillip announced a High Court challenge to Dominica's buggery and sexual-activity provisions at a news conference on 20 July 2019, five years before the provisions were struck down.

Activists greeted the judgment as a significant milestone in the ongoing struggle for LGBTQ rights in the Caribbean (BBC, 23 April 2024).

Dominica is on record as one of 85 countries that signed the 2011 Human Rights Council joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity. It is the only commitment in this inventory that names gender identity expressly alongside sexual orientation.

A senior local religious authority publicly opposed criminalisation in 2013: Catholic Bishop Gabriel Malzaire called for eliminating criminal penalties for homosexuality and for all forms of violence against LGBT people, citing the Holy See's position.
tangentialFactors:
The 2024 ruling addresses sexual-conduct provisions. Nothing in the sources indicates that the judgment or the Act extends equivalent treatment to gender identity, and the only instrument naming gender identity is the non-binding 2011 joint statement Dominica signed.

Human Rights Watch's demand that every Caribbean nation repeal comparable laws indicates that Dominica's decriminalisation runs against the regional current rather than with it, which shapes what a visitor encounters elsewhere in the area.

Decriminalisation here arrived through the judiciary. Legislative bodies did not enact the change, so any parliamentary follow-through, replacement provision or appeal is a separate question from the ruling itself.

Public positions in Dominica are not uniform: an international human rights organisation, a local advocacy founder and a Catholic bishop have each pressed against criminalisation at different points between 2011 and 2024, while the underlying provisions remained in force until 2024.
localsOnly:
MiRiDom, founded by Daryl Phillip, pursued the constitutional challenge to the buggery and sexual-activity provisions and publicised its filing at a news conference on 20 July 2019. Local outlet Dominica News Online reported the filing at the time.

Catholic Bishop Gabriel Malzaire of Dominica spoke against criminal penalties and against violence toward LGBT people in May 2013, invoking the Holy See's position, which gives residents a documented statement of position from the country's leading Catholic authority.

Residents live under a statute whose sections 14 and 16 were nullified by court order rather than amended by parliament, leaving the Sexual Offences Act's text as it stands alongside the constitutional reading imposed on it.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses legal gender recognition, amendment of gender markers on birth certificates, passports or other identity documents, or any process a trans resident would use to change them. This is unresolved, not established either way.

Entry and visa screening, including any interview or inspection that could disclose trans status, is not sourced for Dominica here. Likewise unsourced: hate-crime or anti-discrimination protection expressly covering gender identity, access to gender-affirming medical care, rules on public facilities, and marriage or partner recognition.

Whether the April 2024 judgment was appealed, legislated on, or supplemented by further provisions is not documented in the available sources. Enforcement practice after the ruling is also not sourced.

A 2011 US State Department press statement on Dominica is carried in the inventory but supplies no substantive detail usable for a visitor risk assessment, so it supports only the existence of a diplomatic record, not a finding.

The 2011 joint statement is a declaration by signatory states, not an enforceable instrument, and the sources do not describe any monitoring of Dominica's compliance with it.
